title: The Lucena position: the bridge
summary: Rook and pawn against rook: the position that wins, the bridge that takes the pawn to a queen, and how to get there.
part.lucena.title: The Lucena position
part.lucena.summary: The picture of the winning position, why the king is stuck in front of the pawn, and the two preparatory moves.
part.bridge.title: The bridge
part.bridge.summary: The king steps out and walks down next to the pawn, takes the checks and, on the fifth rank, the rook closes the bridge.
part.fourth.title: The fourth rank, not the fifth
part.fourth.summary: Why the rook waits on the fourth rank: with the black king close, a bridge on the fifth walks into a trap.
part.rook4.title: The black rook on the fourth
part.rook4.summary: When the black rook takes the fourth rank, the king walks out without a bridge: a rook too close cannot check forever.
part.reach.title: Reaching the Lucena
part.reach.summary: Pawn on the fifth, rook cutting off: the pawn advances to take f7 from the black king, and the king climbs behind the checks to the queening square.
part.trade.title: Trading into the Lucena
part.trade.summary: Andersson vs Åkesson, 1999: two pawns become one, the black king stays cut off and the road to the Lucena is forced.
part.rookPawn.title: Rook pawn: when it still wins
part.rookPawn.summary: With a rook pawn, the Lucena wins if the rook is already on the fourth rank and White has the move, or with the black king cut off far away.
part.zugzwang.title: Losing a tempo with the rook
part.zugzwang.summary: Topalov vs Karpov, 2002: no bridge in sight, so the rook dances on the h-file to hand the move back to Black, who must give way. Recap and final practice.
step.t_lucena: Pawn on the seventh, your king in front of it on the queening square, and the black king cut off by your rook. Before any explanation, count your king's moves. Which piece holds it on each side?
step.t_lucena.hint1: c7 and c8 belong to the black king; a7 and a8 to the black rook. Your king has no move at all.
step.t_lucena.hint2: Your rook can drive one of the two away. Which one, and with what move?
step.key: This is the Lucena position. Keep the picture: the pawn on the seventh, your king in front of it on the queening square; the black rook holds your king from the side, and your rook cuts the black king off by at least one file. This is a win, whoever is to move. Karsten Müller says it may be the most important position in all of endgame theory.
step.stuck: The problem is getting out from in front of the pawn. Right now the king has no move: c7 and c8 belong to the black king, a7 and a8 to the rook. That is why the first move is 1.Rd1+, which drives the black king away and opens c7. But opening the door is not enough: on c7 the checks come from the side and, with no shelter, the king goes back to b8. Watch.
step.stuckDemo: I will step out with the king without preparing anything, so you can see why it fails.
step.stuckDemo.m1: 1.Rd1+. The check drives the black king off the c-file, and c7 is free.
step.stuckDemo.m2: 1...Ke7. The black king stays close, two files from the pawn, ready to come back.
step.stuckDemo.m3: 2.Kc7, and the king has left the pawn's square. It looks like it is going to work.
step.stuckDemo.m4: 2...Rc2+. The rook checks from far away, and my king has no shelter anywhere on the c-file.
step.stuckDemo.m5: 3.Kb8, back again. Without shelter from the checks the king steps out and steps back: no progress. The bridge solves this.
step.push: Two preparatory moves. First, drive the black king one more file away, with check. Then lift the rook to the fourth rank: it is going to be the shelter.
step.push.hint: A rook check on the d-file pushes the king away; then the rook goes up to d4.
step.push.done: That's it. The black king is two files from the pawn and the rook waits on the fourth rank. Now your king can come out.
step.t_bridge: The rook waits on d4 and Black has made a waiting move. Now the king comes out. Which way does it go, and what does it do at each check?
step.t_bridge.hint1: Always next to the pawn, one rank at a time: c7, then b6, then c6.
step.t_bridge.hint2: On the fifth rank the king stands just above the rook. Look at what the rook can do about the next check.
step.bridgeIdea: The idea of the bridge: the king walks down the c- and b-files, always right next to the pawn. Each check costs Black a move and the king comes down one rank. When it reaches the fifth, the rook that was waiting on d4 steps in on b4 and blocks the check. Nimzowitsch called this building a bridge, in My System, 1925: the rook is the bridge under which the king crosses.
step.bridgeDemo: Watch the bridge move by move.
step.bridgeDemo.m1: 1.Kc7, through the door that 1.Rd1+ opened: a7 and a8 belong to the black rook. Now the king starts walking down.
step.bridgeDemo.m2: 1...Rc1+. The check on the c-file; if the king goes back to b8, it repeats the story from before.
step.bridgeDemo.m3: 2.Kb6, right next to the pawn: the king protects it and comes down one rank.
step.bridgeDemo.m4: 2...Rb1+. Check on the b-file, which also eyes the pawn: if the king lets go of b7, the rook takes it.
step.bridgeDemo.m5: 3.Kc6. c6 or a6, it does not matter; what matters is coming down one more rank without leaving the pawn.
step.bridgeDemo.m6: 3...Rc1+. The rook keeps at it, but each check brings me closer to my own rook.
step.bridgeDemo.m7: 4.Kb5: the fifth rank, just above my rook. The bridge is about to close.
step.bridgeDemo.m8: 4...Rb1+. The last check: between the black rook and my king lies b4, and my rook gets there in one move.
step.bridgeDemo.m9: 5.Rb4! The bridge. If the rook takes on b4, the king recaptures and the pawn queens; if it does not take, the pawn queens anyway. Black has nothing.
step.bridge: Now it is you. Black waits. Step out with the king and walk down the c- and b-files, always next to the pawn, to the fifth rank. When the check comes on b1 with the king on b5, the rook steps in on b4.
step.bridge.hint: The king goes c7, b6, c6, b5, always next to the pawn. On the fifth rank, the rook blocks the check on b4.
step.bridge.done: The bridge. The black rook has no more checks, and nothing is left to hold the pawn.
step.finish: Now the whole Lucena, with the d-pawn. Drive the black king away, lift the rook, come out with the king and close the bridge. Take the pawn to a queen.
step.t_fourth: The same bridge, but the black king has come closer: it stands on e6. 1.Rd5 would close the bridge right now, one rank higher. Is it good?
step.t_fourth.hint1: Where is the black king in relation to d5? Count how many moves it needs to get there.
step.t_fourth.hint2: If your rook leaves the fourth rank, what does the black rook do with the pawn on b7?
step.whyFourth: Why the fourth rank, and not the fifth? Because the black king comes closer. From e6 it cannot reach d4, but it can reach d5. 1.Rd5 now would be a serious mistake. Watch what happens.
step.trapDemo: I played Rd5. It is Black's move.
step.trapDemo.m1: 1...Rxb7. The black rook gives itself for the pawn, because it knows what comes next.
step.trapDemo.m2: 2.Kxb7. I take the rook, but mine is on d5, right next to the black king.
step.trapDemo.m3: 2...Kxd5. The black king eats the rook. King against king: a draw. The rook on the fifth was within the king's reach; on the fourth it would not have been.
step.trapRight: So how do we solve it? First a check on the sixth rank, to drive the black king away from the rook; only then does the rook go to the fifth. The rest is the bridge you already know, one rank higher: king b6, and the rook closes on b5.
step.trap: Now you. Check on the sixth, rook to the fifth, and the bridge one rank higher.
step.trap.hint: First the check on d6, pushing the king to the seventh. Then 2.Rd5, king b6, and the rook blocks on b5.
step.trap.done: Well done. The bridge works on the fifth rank too, as long as the black king cannot reach the rook.
step.t_rook4: The Lucena position, with Black to move. Black is going to play 1...Ra4 and forbid your rook from going up to d4. What changes in your plan?
step.t_rook4.hint1: A rook far from the king can check forever. A close one cannot: from the fourth rank, after two checks it is within the king's reach.
step.rook4: The black rook on the fourth rank: the defence that looks cleverest. Your bridge on the fourth no longer exists. No harm done: the black rook is too close, and the king walks out right now, with no bridge. The checks run out by themselves.
step.emms: Emms' line. Watch the checks run out.
step.emms.m1: 1...Ra4. The black rook takes the fourth rank: 3.Rd4 is forbidden.
step.emms.m2: 2.Rd1+. The same first move: I drive the black king one more file away.
step.emms.m3: 2...Ke7. The black king stays close, as before.
step.emms.m4: 3.Kc7. The king walks out with no bridge at all.
step.emms.m5: 3...Rc4+. Check on the c-file, from the fourth rank.
step.emms.m6: 4.Kb6, next to the pawn. The only other square was back on b8, and I would be where I started.
step.emms.m7: 4...Rb4+. One more check, but the rook is already two ranks from my king, almost within its reach.
step.emms.m8: 5.Ka6, next to the pawn. The checks are over: the rook on b4 gives no check to a king on a6, and if it checks on a4 the king goes to b5 and attacks it.
step.rook4Why: The checks are over, but the black rook still watches the b-file: if I queen now, it takes on b8 and it is rook against rook. A draw. The file still has to be closed: the white rook goes to d5, takes the two checks that are left and steps in on b5, in front of the black rook. The bridge on the fifth, once again.
step.rook4move: Now you close the b-file. Rook to the fifth rank, the king answers the check next to the pawn, and the rook steps in on b5.
step.rook4move.hint: 1.Rd5 first. On the check from a2, the king goes to b6; on the check from b2, the rook blocks on b5.
step.rook4move.done: Closed. The black rook has no checks, the b-file is yours, and the pawn queens.
step.t_reach: Now from further away: the pawn is still on the fifth, your king beside it and the rook cuts the black king off along the f-file. Which comes first: the pawn or the king?
step.t_reach.hint1: If the king goes to f5 first, the black king steps into f7 and the pawn gets no further. Which move takes f7 away from the black king?
step.t_reach.hint2: After the pawn, the king climbs the g- and h-files, using the pawn as a shield against the checks.
step.reachIdea: Before the bridge comes the road to the Lucena. The rook never leaves the f-file: it is what cuts the black king off. The pawn goes to g6, so that f7 is no square for the black king. And the king climbs against the checks, one rank at a time, until it stands in front of the pawn on the queening square. Then the pawn goes to the seventh, and it is the Lucena.
step.reachDemo: A rook-ending training position. Watch the order.
step.reachDemo.m1: 1.g6! The pawn first: f7 is now attacked, and the black king cannot step into it.
step.reachDemo.m3: 2.Kh5. The king climbs the h-file, beside the pawn.
step.reachDemo.m4: 2...Rh2+. Check again, now on the h-file: the king cannot stay on the rook's file and goes back to the g-file.
step.reachDemo.m5: 3.Kg5. The king returns to the g-file, one rank higher. Each check costs me nothing: I climb.
step.reachDemo.m6: 3...Rg2+. The rook keeps at it, and the king has to leave the g-file. The right square is on the h-file, next to the pawn: on f4 or f5 the king would block my own rook, and the win would slip away.
step.reachDemo.m7: 4.Kh6. Sixth rank, beside the pawn, which is protected.
step.reachDemo.m8: 4...Rh2+. The last useful check: the king goes into g7, in front of the pawn, and on the g-file the rook can no longer check, because the pawn is in the way.
step.reachDemo.m9: 5.Kg7. The king in front of the pawn, on the seventh. From g7 it watches f7, f8 and g8.
step.reachDemo.m10: 5...Rg2. Out of checks, the black rook goes back to holding the pawn. What is left is to bring the king to g8 and the pawn to g7.
step.reachMove: Finish the road. The king goes to g8 via the h-file, and the pawn goes up to the seventh. Recognise the position when it appears.
step.reachMove.hint: 1.Kh7 first: from h7 the king still protects the pawn (from g8 it would not: 1...Rxg6+). On the check from h2, 2.Kg8; then 3.g7.
step.reachMove.done: The Lucena, on the kingside. The black rook holds from the side and your rook cuts the black king off. The rest you know: check, rook to the fourth, bridge.
step.t_trade: The ending of Ulf Andersson against Ralf Åkesson, Skellefteå, 1999. Two moves earlier it was two pawns against one; Andersson traded, and here, with Black to move, Åkesson resigned. Why? Find White's plan against the checks.
step.t_trade.hint1: The black king is cut off along the e-file. The f-pawn always advances with the king beside it and, when the king stands in front of it on the seventh, it is the Lucena.
step.anderssonIntro: Andersson had two pawns, e and f, against one. Instead of keeping the material, he traded the e-pawn to be left with a single one, but with the black king cut off and the f-pawn escorted by the king. Trading into a position you know is won: that is what the Lucena is worth. His opponent resigned here. Watch the continuation the commentators give.
step.anderssonRoad: Black checks; the king hides beside the pawn.
step.anderssonRoad.m1: 81...Rg1+. The black rook starts the checks on the g-file.
step.anderssonRoad.m2: 82.Kf7. The king in front of the pawn, and the black rook has no check on the f-file.
step.anderssonRoad.m3: 82...Rf1. The rook goes back to holding the pawn.
step.anderssonRoad.m4: 83.f6. The pawn advances, protected by the king.
step.anderssonRoad.m5: 83...Rf2. The black rook waits behind the pawn.
step.anderssonRoad.m6: 84.Kg7, beside the pawn, clearing the way to f7.
step.anderssonRoad.m7: 84...Rg2+. Check on the g-file. The answer is to step in front of the pawn: on f8, the pawn itself shields me from checks on the f-file.
step.anderssonRoad.m8: 85.Kf8. The king in front of the pawn, on the queening square.
step.anderssonRoad.m9: 85...Rf2. The black rook holds the pawn again.
step.anderssonRoad.m10: 86.f7. The pawn on the seventh, the king in front of it.
step.anderssonRoad.m11: 86...Rg2. Do you recognise it? King on the queening square, pawn on the seventh, the black rook holding from the side and your rook cutting the black king off along the e-file. It is the Lucena, with the f-pawn.
step.anderssonLucena: It is worth trading material to reach a position you know is won. Here the bridge is on the kingside, and one move does both preparations at once: 1.Rd4+ drives the black king one more file away and already leaves the rook on the fourth rank. Then the king walks down via e7, f6, e6, f5, and the rook closes on f4.
step.anderssonBridge: Build Andersson's bridge. Check on the fourth rank, the king walks down the e- and f-files, always next to the pawn, and the rook closes on f4.
step.anderssonBridge.hint: 1.Rd4+ drives the king away and lifts the rook. Then the king goes e7, f6, e6, f5, and the rook blocks on f4.
step.anderssonBridge.done: The bridge on the kingside. Andersson never had to play it: his opponent saw it coming.
step.t_rookPawn: A rook pawn, which the rule says does not win: in the corner the king has only one side to come out on. But here, with White to move, it wins; with Black to move, it is a draw. Why?
step.t_rookPawn.hint1: Your rook is already on the fourth rank. In one move it reaches a4, behind the pawn.
step.t_rookPawn.hint2: The king comes out now, before the black rook gets organised. If it were Black's move, 1...Rb1 would forbid b7 and it would be a draw.
step.rookPawnRule: The rule: with a rook pawn, the Lucena wins only if the white rook is already on the fourth rank, the black rook is not on the file next to the pawn, and White has the move. The king steps out to b7 at once; when the black rook leaves the a-file, your rook goes to a4, behind the pawn, and the a-file becomes yours. With any of the three missing, Black holds, unless the black king is cut off far away, as in the next position.
step.rookPawnDemo.m1: 1.Kb7. The king leaves the corner now. The black rook is still on a1 and does not control b7.
step.rookPawnDemo.m2: 1...Rb1+. Check on the b-file: the king only has a6 or the corner, a8, and going back to the corner would throw the win away.
step.rookPawnDemo.m3: 2.Ka6, next to the pawn. If the rook returns to a1 with check, the king goes to b6 and nothing has changed.
step.rookPawnDemo.m4: 2...Rc1. The black rook changes plan: it wants to reach c8 and watch the queening square.
step.rookPawnDemo.m5: 3.Ra4! The rook was already on the fourth rank: in one move it gets behind the pawn. The a-file is mine, and the pawn is protected.
step.rookPawnDemo.m6: 3...Rc8. The black rook watches a8: if the pawn queens now, it takes the queen, and my king on a6 blocks my rook's file.
step.rookPawnDemo.m7: 4.Kb6. The king steps out of the way, and the rook looks after the pawn.
step.rookPawnDemo.m8: 4...Rc6+. The last check. It takes the black rook off c8: for one move, nobody watches a8.
step.rookPawnDemo.m9: 5.Kb5. The king escapes and still protects the rook.
step.rookPawnDemo.m10: 5...Rc8. Back to watching a8, but with no checks.
step.rookPawnDemo.m11: 6.a8=Q. The black rook has to give itself for the queen, and it is rook against king. With Black to move in the starting position, none of this existed: 1...Rb1 forbade b7.
step.silman: The other chance with a rook pawn: the black king cut off far away, four files from the pawn. A position by Silman. The rook goes in front of the pawn, to b8, so the king can come out via b7; then the king walks against the checks towards the black king, and at the end there is a rook sacrifice, which you will discover in the exercises.
step.rookPawnFar: Bring the rook to the b-file, in front of the pawn: c1, c8 and b8.
step.rookPawnFar.hint: The rook goes round via c1 and c8 to reach b8. 1.Rb1 straight away does not work: the black rook captures and your king has no move, stalemate.
step.rookPawnFar.done: 3.Rb8: now the king comes out via b7. The rest is the king's walk against the checks, via c8 and d8, with a sacrifice at the end.
step.t_zugzwang: The ending of Veselin Topalov against Anatoly Karpov, Cannes, 2002. Pawn on the seventh and your king in front of it, but the black king is glued to d8 and Black still has the h-pawn, which your rook watches. No bridge in sight. What does White need?
step.t_zugzwang.hint1: If it were Black's move, which Black move would not make something worse? Try them all.
step.t_zugzwang.hint2: Your rook cannot let go of the h-pawn. Can it lose a tempo without leaving the h-file?
step.zugzwangIdea: This is zugzwang: the obligation to move. In this position, if it were Black's move, any move would spoil something: the rook cannot leave the a-file, the king cannot leave the pawn, and the h-pawn, if it advances, falls. So White needs to hand the move back. The rook does it without leaving the h-file: check on h8, the king returns to d7, the rook returns to h6. And now it is Black to move.
step.tempoDemo: Topalov's move, and the end of the game.
step.tempoDemo.m1: 71.Rh8+. Check; the rook keeps watching the h-pawn.
step.tempoDemo.m2: 71...Kd7. The black king returns next to the pawn; e7 would be even worse.
step.tempoDemo.m3: 72.Rh6. The rook back on the sixth, and now it is Black to move. Zugzwang: any move gives something up.
step.tempoDemo.m4: 72...Kd8. Karpov chose the king: the rook stays on the a-file and the h-pawn stays where it is.
step.tempoDemo.m5: 73.Rh7. The rook watches the seventh rank: the black king cannot go back to d7, and Black is in zugzwang again.
step.tempoDemo.m6: 73...Rb4. The black rook leaves the a-file to attack the pawn. That was all I needed.
step.tempoDemo.m7: 74.Ka7. The king comes out along the a-file, which has been left free.
step.tempoDemo.m8: 74...Ra4+. Black needs to give check: without it, 75.b8=Q next move.
step.tempoDemo.m9: 75.Kb6. The king protects the pawn and the checks are over: on 75...Rb4+ the king goes to c6, still next to the pawn; on c5 it would leave it, and the rook would hold it again. Karpov resigned.
step.zugzwangWhy: Why does no Black move work? The rook has to stay on the a-file: if it leaves, 73.Ka7 and the king escapes. The king has to stay on d7 or d8: if it goes to the e-file, my king gains c7, and the checks along the seventh and eighth ranks follow it. And the h-pawn, if it advances, is captured; without it, the white rook goes up to the fourth rank and it is the usual Lucena.
step.recap: Four rules to take with you. One: king in front of the pawn on the queening square, enemy king cut off, is the Lucena. Two: check to drive the king away and rook to the fourth rank; the fifth only with the black king far away. Three: the king walks down next to the pawn and the rook closes the bridge; if the black rook is too close, the king walks out with no bridge. Four: with a rook pawn, it only wins with the rook already on the fourth and the move, or with the black king cut off four files away. And remember: not every position that looks like this wins. The black rook far away, on the long side, is the short-side lesson.
step.tempoPlay: Finish like Topalov. Black has just played Kd8, back into the zugzwang. Hand the move back once more, take the king out on whichever side opens, and bring the pawn to a queen.
ex.e12: White to play and win. A king's pawn, and the black rook reached the fourth rank first: there is no bridge there. How does White make progress?
ex.e12.hint: First drive the black king away with a check. Then ask whether your king really needs shelter: the black rook is too close to keep checking for long.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Rc1+ drives the king to b7, and 2.Kd7! walks out at once, with no bridge. The checks soon run out: 2...Rd4+ 3.Ke6, 3...Re4+ 4.Kd6, and the white rook comes back along the d-file (5.Rd1, 6.Rd5+) to shut the road on the fifth rank. Other moves also win, but walking out with the king is the shortest road: with the black rook so close, the king needs no bridge. Hawkins' line.
ex.e13: White to play and win. Andersson vs Åkesson, Skellefteå, 1999. Two pawns against one, but the clearest road goes through a position you already know.
ex.e13.hint: With a single pawn, which position do you want on the board? Look for a pawn trade that leaves the black king cut off.
ex.e13.solution: 79.e4! After 79...dxe4 80.Rxe4, the black king is cut off by the rook and the f-pawn, with the white king beside it, goes on to the Lucena. The game went 80...Kd7 81.Kg6 and Black resigned. 79.Re6+, 79.Re7 and 79.Re8 also win, but 79.e4 is Andersson's idea: trade into the position you know is won.
ex.e14: White to play and win. The pawn is still on the third rank and the black rook is already attacking it. Take the pawn forward without letting the black king come back.
ex.e14.hint: The pawn advances protected by the king, not by the rook. When the black king comes close, the rook cuts it off along the file.
ex.e14.solution: 1.e4! The king on f5 protects the pawn (1.Rb7+ also wins). After 1...Kc5, 2.e5 moves on again, and when the black king reaches d5, 3.Rd7+ cuts it off along the d-file. From there it is the known road: pawn on the seventh, king in front, bridge. Defending the pawn with the rook or moving the king away from f5 draws.
ex.e15: White to play and win. A rook's pawn, which nearly always draws. Here there is a chance, and only because White has the move. Find it.
ex.e15.hint: The black king sits next to the b-file and locks your king in the corner. Push it away first; the rook on the fourth rank does the rest.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Rc4+! drives the black king to d7. Then 2.Kb7 leaves the corner, and after the check on b1 the king goes to a6, next to the pawn: with the rook already on the fourth rank, the checks run out and the pawn promotes. With Black to move, 1...Rc1 or 1...Kc7 holds the draw. With a rook's pawn, the Lucena only wins like this: the rook already on the fourth rank and White to move.
ex.e16: White to play and win. Topalov vs Karpov, Cannes, 2002. The black king is right next to the pawn and Black still has the h-pawn. No bridge in sight. What now?
ex.e16.hint: Your rook cannot let go of the h-pawn. Look for the position where Black, having to move, must give something up.
ex.e16.solution: Topalov played 70.Rh7+ Kd8 71.Rh8+ Kd7 72.Rh6! The starting position again, now with Black to move. It is zugzwang: every Black move makes things worse. The h-pawn falls, the king steps away from the pawn, or the rook leaves the a-file and the white king gets out. The game went 72...Kd8 73.Rh7 Rb4 74.Ka7 Ra4+ 75.Kb6 and Karpov resigned. The rook loses a tempo without leaving the h-file: 70.Rh8 on the first move, or 71.Rh6 and 71.Rh5 on the second, also win.
ex.e17: White to play and win. A rook's pawn again, but now the black king is far away. This is Silman's line, after 1.Rc1 Ke7. Every move counts, right to the end.
ex.e17.hint: The rook goes in front of the pawn, along the b-file, so the king can get out. Then the king walks towards the black king, and at the end there is a sacrifice.
ex.e17.solution: 2.Rc8 and 3.Rb8: the rook on the b-file frees the king. 3...Ra2, and 4.Kb7 steps out; the king escapes the checks via c8 and d8, towards the black king. When the black rook goes to h2, 7.Rb6+ Kc5 and 8.Rc6+! If 8...Kxc6, 9.a8=Q+ and it is queen against rook, which wins; if the king runs, the rook goes back and the pawn promotes. With a rook's pawn, it only wins with the black king cut off far away.
key.lucena: The Lucena position as Alessandro Salvio published it in 1634: the pawn is one step from promoting and the white king stands in front of it. White wins whoever moves: all that is left is to build the bridge.
key.villa5: Another Lucena, with the black king further away. The rook can build the bridge on the fourth rank, the safest way, but the fifth works too.
key.rook4: The Lucena position with Black to move: the black rook goes to the fourth rank and stops the bridge there. White still wins by building it one rank higher.
key.shortSide: The exception: Black is to move, and the black rook, far from the pawn, checks from the side without end. A draw. This is the short-side lesson's defence.
key.practiceBridge: The Lucena on the other side of the board: the rook gives one check to push the black king away, goes to the fourth rank and from there becomes the bridge.
key.andersson: Andersson vs Åkesson, 1999: Black resigned here. The white king is beside the pawn, and nothing can stop the Lucena position from appearing.
key.rookPawn: With a rook pawn the Lucena does not always win. Here everything depends on the move: with White to play, the king gets out of the corner in time and wins; with Black to play, the rook traps the king and draws.
key.topalov: Topalov vs Karpov, 2002: there was no way to build a bridge. With three rook moves White handed the move back, and Karpov, with nothing good to play, resigned.
history: The Lucena position is the most important one in rook endings: with rook and pawn against rook it is the position that wins, and almost every ending of this kind revolves around reaching it or preventing it. The name is a historical mistake: the Spaniard Luis Ramírez de Lucena wrote one of the first printed chess books around 1497, but the position is not in it; it first appears in 1634, in a book by the Italian Alessandro Salvio. The idea of "building a bridge" with the rook, which is the heart of this lesson, got its name from Aron Nimzowitsch in 1925. Grandmasters know it so well that they rarely need to play it out: in 1999, in Sweden, Ulf Andersson exchanged pawns just to reach it, and his opponent resigned before the bridge ever appeared on the board. In 2002, in Cannes, Veselin Topalov beat Anatoly Karpov in a similar position where no bridge was possible, with a trick to hand over the move.
practice: Now the real ending: rook and pawn against rook, with your king far away and the black rook active. Bring the king in front of the pawn, cut the black king off and look for the Lucena. I will be checking the bridge.
